title: Time and the Conways
description: Priestley's finest play: a family in 1919, in 1937 and again in 1919, and the failure of the future to arrive.
plot_or_argument: At a birthday party in 1919 the Conway family are full of promise; in act two, set in 1937, the promise has collapsed into failure and bitterness; act three returns to 1919, when the young Kay sees what is coming.
narrative_structure: Three acts, 1919, 1937 and 1919 again.
principal_characters: Kay Conway; Mrs Conway; Alan Conway; Hazel Conway; Madge Conway; Robin Conway; Carol Conway; Joan Helford; Ernest Beevers
historical_context: The English middle class between the wars, the slump and the lost generation of the twenties.
literary_significance: Time and the Conways is Priestley's finest play and the clearest statement of his theory of time: its structure and its portrait of a family's disappointment made it one of the great English plays of the decade.

title: An Inspector Calls
description: The most performed English play of the century: the Birling family, the inspector and the girl who died.
plot_or_argument: The Birling family are celebrating the engagement of their daughter when Inspector Goole arrives to question them about the suicide of Eva Smith; each member of the family is shown to have contributed to her destruction, and the inspector's identity and the play's final telephone call leave the family — and the audience — under judgment.
narrative_structure: Three acts, in real time, in the Birlings' dining room.
principal_characters: Inspector Goole; Arthur Birling; Sybil Birling; Sheila Birling; Eric Birling; Gerald Croft; Edna
historical_context: The English industrial middle class of 1912, and the postwar moment of 1945 when the play was written and first performed.
literary_significance: An Inspector Calls is the most performed English play of the century and Priestley's masterpiece: its structure, its moral argument and its famous ending made it a permanent part of the world theatre.

title: The Good Companions
description: The great English picaresque of the twenties: a concert party on the road and three lives changed by it.
plot_or_argument: Jess Oakroyd, a Yorkshire mill hand, Miss Trant, a middle-aged spinster, and Inigo Jollifant, a schoolmaster, all join a touring concert party, the Dinky Doos, and travel the English provinces through comedy, failure and success.
narrative_structure: A picaresque novel in six parts, following the concert party on tour.
principal_characters: Jess Oakroyd; Elizabeth Trant; Inigo Jollifant; Susie Dean; Jimmy Nunn; Morton Mitcham
historical_context: The English provinces in the late 1920s, the concert party and the music hall, and the North of England.
literary_significance: The Good Companions is the great English picaresque of the twenties and Priestley's most popular novel: its warmth, its provincial comedy and its portrait of the touring company made it a bestseller and the founding text of the English road novel.

title: Angel Pavement
description: Priestley's London novel: a City firm, a mysterious stranger and the lives of the clerks.
plot_or_argument: In the offices of Twigg and Dersingham, a firm of veneer merchants in the City, the arrival of the mysterious Mr Golspie transforms the business and the lives of the clerks — the ambitious Mr Dersingham, the clerk Mr Smeeth and the typist Turgis — before the crash and the disappearance.
narrative_structure: A novel of the office and the City, following several lives through a year.
principal_characters: Mr Golspie; Mr Dersingham; Mr Smeeth; Turgis; Lilian Matfield; Poppy
historical_context: The City of London in 1930, the Depression and the lives of the lower middle class.
literary_significance: Angel Pavement is Priestley's London novel and his finest: its portrait of the City, its sympathy for the clerks and its picture of the slump made it one of the great English novels of the Depression.

title: The Winslow Boy
description: Rattigan's masterpiece: a father's fight to clear his son's name, and the cost to the family.
plot_or_argument: Ronnie Winslow is expelled from the Royal Naval College for stealing a postal order; his father, Arthur Winslow, takes the case to the House of Lords through the barrister Sir Robert Morton, and the family is changed by the struggle — his daughter's engagement broken, his wife's health ruined, and the boy's own innocence consumed.
narrative_structure: Four acts, in the Winslows' drawing room.
principal_characters: Arthur Winslow; Ronnie Winslow; Catherine Winslow; Sir Robert Morton; Grace Winslow; Dickie Winslow; Violet; Desmond Curry
historical_context: England before the First World War, the naval college, and the Edwardian family.
literary_significance: The Winslow Boy is Rattigan's masterpiece and one of the finest English plays of the century: its treatment of justice, family and the price of principle made it a permanent part of the repertory.

title: The Browning Version
description: The finest one-act play in English: a hated schoolmaster's last day, and the boy who gives him a book.
plot_or_argument: Andrew Crocker-Harris, a classics master at a public school, is being retired after eighteen years of unpopularity; on his last day his wife betrays him, his headmaster humiliates him, and a boy gives him a gift of the Browning translation that restores his dignity.
narrative_structure: A single act, set in the sitting room of a schoolmaster's house.
principal_characters: Andrew Crocker-Harris; Millie Crocker-Harris; Frank Hunter; John Taplow; the Headmaster
historical_context: The English public school just after the Second World War.
literary_significance: The Browning Version is the finest one-act play in English and Rattigan's masterpiece: its portrait of the unloved schoolmaster and its final scene made it one of the great achievements of the English stage.

title: Separate Tables
description: Rattigan's double bill of loneliness: a hotel dining room and the people who eat alone.
plot_or_argument: In the dining room of a Bournemouth residential hotel, 'Table by the Window' follows a disgraced politician and his former wife, and 'Table Number Seven' a shy major with a scandal in his past; the two plays share the same set and the same hotel.
narrative_structure: Two one-act plays sharing the hotel dining room.
principal_characters: Major Pollock; Miss Railton-Bell; Sibyl Railton-Bell; Anne Shankland; John Malcolm; Mabel
historical_context: The English residential hotel and the genteel poor of the early 1950s.
literary_significance: Separate Tables is Rattigan's double bill of loneliness and one of the finest plays of the postwar English stage: its two studies of quiet desperation made the hotel dining room a permanent theatrical setting.

title: Seven Pillars of Wisdom
description: The great English prose epic of the desert war: Lawrence of Arabia and the Arab Revolt.
plot_or_argument: Lawrence's memoir of the Arab Revolt against the Ottoman Empire in 1916–18: the campaigns with Feisal and Auda abu Tayi, the raids on Aqaba and the Hejaz railway, the capture of Damascus, and his own self-examination as the leader of other men in a war he has come to doubt.
narrative_structure: Ten books, from the Arab Revolt's beginning to the capture of Damascus.
principal_characters: T. E. Lawrence; Prince Feisal; Auda abu Tayi; General Allenby; Ali ibn el Hussein
historical_context: The Arab Revolt of 1916–1918, the collapse of the Ottoman Empire, and the imperial settlement of the Middle East.
literary_significance: Seven Pillars of Wisdom is the great English prose epic of the desert war and one of the finest memoirs in the language: its prose, its self-scrutiny and its portrait of the Arab revolt made it the permanent literary record of the war in the desert and the founding text of the modern literature of the Middle East.

title: The Mint
description: Lawrence's private record of life as an aircraftman: the making of a soldier in the ranks.
plot_or_argument: Written in 1922–23 and published after his death, The Mint records Lawrence's life as an aircraftman in the Royal Air Force: the barrack room, the drill square, the bullies and the camaraderie, and the destruction of the individual in the machine of military training.
narrative_structure: Three parts: the Depot, the training and the service.
principal_characters: Lawrence (as 352087 A/c Ross); the flight sergeant; the recruits
historical_context: The Royal Air Force of 1922 and the postwar demobilisation.
literary_significance: The Mint is the most pitiless record of military training in English: its prose and its refusal of self-pity made it a radical document of the machine age and the dark companion to Seven Pillars.

title: The Complete Short Stories of Saki
description: The collected stories of the finest English comic writer of the short story: Clovis, Reginald and the wolves.
plot_or_argument: The volume gathers Munro's stories — 'Sredni Vashtar', 'The Open Window', 'Tobermory', 'The Interlopers', 'The Schartz-Metterklume Method' — in which children, animals and the Wildean epigram take revenge on the English middle class.
narrative_structure: A collected edition of the stories, with a memoir by Ethel Munro.
principal_characters: Clovis Sangrail; Reginald; Vera; Conradin; Tobermory; the Interlopers
historical_context: Edwardian England, the country house, and the years before the First World War in which Munro was killed.
literary_significance: The Complete Short Stories of Saki gathers the finest comic short stories in English: Munro's wit, his cruelty and his perfect construction made him the master of the English short story, and his influence on Waugh, Wodehouse and the modern comic story is beyond measure.

title: Beasts and Super-Beasts
description: Saki's finest collection: 'The Open Window', 'Sredni Vashtar' and the revenge of the young.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'The Open Window', 'Sredni Vashtar', 'The Schartz-Metterklume Method', 'The Story-Teller', 'Tobermory' and 'The Interlopers', in which children, animals and practical jokers overturn the certainties of their elders.
narrative_structure: Thirty-six stories in a single collection.
principal_characters: Vera; Conradin; Mrs Sappleton; Clovis Sangrail; Tobermory
historical_context: Edwardian England and the country-house world of the years before the First World War.
literary_significance: Beasts and Super-Beasts is Saki's finest collection and the central text of the English comic short story: it contains 'The Open Window' and 'Sredni Vashtar', two of the most anthologised stories in the language.

title: Love on the Dole
description: The great novel of the Depression: Salford, unemployment and the destruction of a family.
plot_or_argument: Harry Hardcastle leaves school in 1926 and finds no work but the dole; his father is crippled in the mill, his sister is driven to the streets, and the family is broken by unemployment in a Salford slum in the years of the Depression.
narrative_structure: A novel in four parts, following the family through the Depression.
principal_characters: Harry Hardcastle; Sally Hardcastle; Mr Hardcastle; Mrs Hardcastle; Larry Meath; Helen
historical_context: Salford and the industrial North in the Depression of the early 1930s, and the means test.
literary_significance: Love on the Dole is the great English novel of the Depression and the finest proletarian novel of the period: its documentary accuracy and its anger made it the most influential book of the 1930s and it was banned by the BBC and adapted into a celebrated play.

title: Our Irish Theatre: A Chapter of Autobiography
description: Lady Gregory's account of the founding of the Abbey Theatre and the fight for an Irish drama.
plot_or_argument: Lady Gregory tells the history of the Irish Literary Theatre and the Abbey from the inside: the first productions, the riots over The Playboy, the tours to America, and the arguments with the Castle and the Church over censorship.
narrative_structure: A memoir in chapters, from the first productions to the American tours.
principal_characters: Lady Gregory; W. B. Yeats; J. M. Synge; Edward Martyn; the Abbey company
historical_context: Dublin in the years 1899 to 1913, the Irish literary revival and the controversy over Synge's plays.
literary_significance: Our Irish Theatre is the essential memoir of the Irish dramatic revival and the only full account written from inside the movement: it recorded the founding of the Abbey and the battle over The Playboy, and it remains the primary source for the period.

title: Visions and Beliefs in the West of Ireland
description: The great collection of Irish folk belief: the fairies, the dead and the second sight, recorded from the mouths of the people.
plot_or_argument: Lady Gregory records, in the words of the country people of Galway and Clare, their beliefs about the fairies, the banshee, the dead, the evil eye and the second sight, with notes on the survival of paganism in the Irish countryside.
narrative_structure: Two volumes of recorded testimony with notes and commentary.
principal_characters: The people of Galway and Clare; Lady Gregory as collector
historical_context: The west of Ireland at the turn of the century, the oral tradition, and the folklore movement of the revival.
literary_significance: Visions and Beliefs in the West of Ireland is the great collection of Irish folk belief and the finest work of folklore to come out of the Irish revival: its fidelity to the spoken word made it a primary source for Yeats, for Synge and for every later student of Irish tradition.

title: Boy
description: The most brutal English novel of the thirties: a Liverpool boy, a ship and the sea.
plot_or_argument: Thirteen-year-old Francis Ferris is taken from his brutal father and sent to sea as a cabin boy; the voyage of the SS Trevithick through the Suez Canal to the Far East becomes an ordeal of beatings, hunger and sexual exploitation, and the novel ends with his death in a dockside brothel.
narrative_structure: A novel in three parts, from Liverpool to the sea and the brothel.
principal_characters: Francis Ferris; Mr Ferris; the captain; the crew of the SS Trevithick
historical_context: Liverpool and the merchant navy in the late 1920s, and the poverty of the English working class.
literary_significance: Boy is the most brutal English novel of the thirties: its unsparing prose and its treatment of the working-class child at sea made it a landmark of the proletarian novel, and it was banned and prosecuted on publication.

title: The Furys
description: Hanley's Liverpool family chronicle: a mother, her sons and the return of the sailor.
plot_or_argument: Mrs Fury waits in Liverpool for her son Peter to return from the sea, while her other sons and daughters struggle with poverty, religion and the threat of the workhouse; the novel is a great chronicle of a working-class Catholic family in the Depression.
narrative_structure: A family chronicle in five parts.
principal_characters: Mrs Fury; Peter Fury; Desmond Fury; Brigid Fury; Denny Fury
historical_context: Liverpool in the early 1930s, the Irish Catholic working class and the Depression.
literary_significance: The Furys is Hanley's Liverpool family chronicle and the finest of his novels: its portrait of the working-class Catholic family made it one of the great achievements of the thirties' proletarian novel.

title: The Wind Among the Reeds
description: Yeats's finest early collection: the symbols of the wind, the reeds, the cloths and the beloved, and the Celtic twilight at its most musical.
plot_or_argument: The collection's poems — 'The Hosting of the Sidhe', 'The Song of Wandering Aengus', 'The Cap and Bells', 'He Wishes for the Cloths of Heaven' — move between the fairy world, the Irish mythic past and the poet's unrequited love for Maud Gonne, and close with the long symbolic poem 'The Binding of the Hair'.
narrative_structure: Thirty-six poems as a symbolic sequence with the poet's own notes.
historical_context: The Ireland of the 1890s, the folklore collections of Lady Gregory and Douglas Hyde, the occult societies (the Golden Dawn, the Theosophists) and the poet's hopeless love for Maud Gonne.
literary_significance: The Wind Among the Reeds is the summit of the Celtic Twilight and the last great book of Yeats's early manner: its symbolism — the sidhe, the cloths, the wandering Aengus — gave Irish poetry a mythological vocabulary, and 'He Wishes for the Cloths of Heaven' is one of the best-known lyric poems in English.

title: The Wild Swans at Coole
description: The book in which Yeats became a modern poet: the middle style, the public poem and 'Easter 1916'.
plot_or_argument: The title poem counts fifty-nine swans on the lake at Lady Gregory's Coole Park and measures the nineteen years since the poet first counted them; the collection also contains 'Easter 1916', 'The Rose Tree', 'In Memory of Major Robert Gregory' and 'On Being Asked for a War Poem'.
narrative_structure: Thirty-one poems, including a long elegy and a political poem in four-line stanzas.
historical_context: The First World War, the Easter Rising of 1916, the death of Major Robert Gregory in Italy, and Yeats's marriage in 1917.
literary_significance: The Wild Swans at Coole is the hinge of Yeats's career: 'Easter 1916' — 'a terrible beauty is born' — is the central Irish political poem of the century, 'In Memory of Major Robert Gregory' is the finest English elegy of the period after 'Lycidas', and the collection marks the moment when the symbolist became the modern poet.

title: The Tower
description: The great late collection of Yeats's old age: the tower at Ballylee, the gyres, Byzantium and the rage against mortality.
plot_or_argument: The collection opens with 'Sailing to Byzantium' and 'The Tower' and includes 'Meditations in Time of Civil War', 'Nineteen Hundred and Nineteen', 'Leda and the Swan', 'Among School Children' and 'A Man Young and Old' — poems of the ageing body, the civil war, the mythic vision and the permanence of art.
narrative_structure: Twenty-five poems in five sections.
historical_context: The Irish Civil War (1922–23) and the Free State, Yeats's Senatorship, the Nobel Prize of 1923, and his Norman tower at Ballylee.
literary_significance: The Tower is Yeats's greatest single collection and the summit of English poetry between The Waste Land and Four Quartets: 'Among School Children', 'Sailing to Byzantium' and 'The Tower' are among the greatest poems in the language.

title: The Countess Cathleen
description: Yeats's first major verse play and the founding production of the Irish literary theatre.
plot_or_argument: During a famine, the Countess Cathleen sells her lands and finally her soul to the demons who are buying Irish souls for corn; the play ends with her death and her salvation by divine mercy. It opened the Irish Literary Theatre in May 1899 and was attacked from the pulpit for its theology.
narrative_structure: Four scenes in verse and prose, with songs.
principal_characters: Countess Cathleen; Aleel; the two demons; Shemus; Teigue; Oona
historical_context: The Irish famine of the 1840s, the folk legends of soul-selling, and the politico-religious controversy of the 1890s.
literary_significance: The Countess Cathleen founded the Irish literary theatre and made the verse play a national form: its opening night in 1899 began the movement that built the Abbey Theatre.
